opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so early on, the thing I cared about most was that people felt heard. When you're building a framework, especially one that's competing with very well-funded alternatives, the community is really your biggest asset. So we thought pretty deliberately about where people would come to ask questions and how fast they'd get a response.

We split things up roughly by intent. GitHub issues were for bugs and feature requests, things that needed to be tracked and acted on by the core team. But we noticed very quickly that if you let usage questions flood into GitHub, the signal-to-noise ratio collapses, and the engineers who need to fix real bugs just drown. So we set up the discussion forum as the place for "how do I do this," "why is my model not converging," that kind of thing. That gave us a searchable, long-lived archive, which turned out to be hugely valuable. A lot of people find answers today from threads that were written years ago.

Then there was the question of who answers. In the beginning, it was literally the core developers, myself included, spending a lot of time on the forums every day. I think that mattered a lot culturally. When a new user asks a question and someone who actually wrote the code answers within a few hours, that sets a tone. People see that the project cares, and they start answering each other's questions too. Over time, the community took on more and more of that load, and some of our most active forum helpers ended up becoming contributors and even maintainers.

We also tried to be thoughtful about real-time channels like Slack or chat. They're great for contributors coordinating, but for user support they're kind of a trap, because the knowledge disappears into scrollback and nobody can search for it later. So we leaned toward async, public, searchable channels for users, and kept the real-time stuff more for people working on the codebase.

The overarching philosophy was: treat support as part of the product. The docs, the error messages, the forum, the issue tracker, they're all part of the user experience. If someone has a frustrating time getting help, that's a product bug just as much as a crash is.

r001.rationale: The response says the forum offered a searchable, long-lived archive, but it does not identify search-engine indexability as a deliberate design requirement.

r002.rationale: It calls real-time chat a poor fit for user support, but says nothing about support expense or restricting Slack access based on users’ PyTorch competence.

r003.rationale: It directs usage questions, including why a model is not converging, to the forum and says chat is a poor fit for user support because its knowledge is hard to find later.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention promoting community projects through PyTorch’s Twitter account.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a lot of it wasn't designed in the way people might imagine, like sitting down with a whiteboard and drawing out a support strategy. It came out of what we actually wanted the experience of using PyTorch to feel like.

When we started, the thing I kept coming back to was that research is already frustrating enough. If you're a grad student trying to get a model to train at two in the morning and you hit some weird error, the last thing you want is to file a GitHub issue and hear back in three weeks. So from very early on we were obsessive about response time. We'd try to respond to issues within hours, not days. Even if the response was just "yeah, this is a real bug, we're looking at it," that acknowledgment mattered a lot. People need to know a human saw it.

The second thing was that we wanted people to be able to ask questions that weren't bugs. GitHub issues are not a great place for "how do I do X" or "is this the right way to think about this." So we set up the discussion forums fairly early, and that turned out to be one of the most important decisions. It gave the community a place to help each other, and over time a lot of the answering was done by people who weren't on the core team at all. Someone like ptrblck basically became a legend on there just by answering thousands of questions carefully and kindly. We didn't plan that. We just created the space and tried to set the tone.

And tone was something I cared about a lot. I'd seen communities where asking a beginner question gets you a sarcastic "read the docs" reply, and that kind of thing compounds. People stop asking, and then they stop using the tool. So we tried to model the opposite from the top. Be generous, assume the person asking is smart and just missing context, and answer the question they're actually asking.

The other piece is Slack and later the dev discussions, which were more for people building on PyTorch or contributing to it. That's a different audience with different needs, and mixing it with beginner questions didn't serve either group well. So separating those channels was deliberate.

If I had to summarize the philosophy, it would be that support isn't a cost center you minimize. It's part of the product. The way people feel when they get stuck is a huge part of whether they come back, and for a framework that lived or died on adoption by researchers, that was everything.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why the forums were useful, but does not mention search-engine indexability as a design requirement.

r002.rationale: It says Slack was aimed at people building on or contributing to PyTorch, but does not say access was limited based on demonstrated competence or that support expense motivated this.

r003.rationale: It places non-bug and beginner questions in the forums, while describing Slack as serving builders and contributors and saying that mixing the audiences did not serve either group.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention promoting community projects through PyTorch’s Twitter account.

astra-6.text:
I thought of user support as part of the product. It’s not enough for the software to be good; when somebody gets stuck, they need a way to get unstuck, and that experience matters a lot.

Different channels serve different purposes. GitHub issues are useful for concrete bugs and feature requests. But if you’re asking, “Why isn’t my model learning?” you want a place where you can have a conversation without having to frame your question as a software defect. A forum also makes those conversations searchable, so the answer helps the next person with the same problem.

The other thing is setting the tone. You want people to feel comfortable asking basic questions. If the developers are patient and helpful, that gives the community an example to follow. Over time, you want users helping one another, because a support system that depends on the core developers answering every question won’t scale.

r001.rationale: The response says forum conversations are searchable, but does not identify search-engine indexability as a deliberate design requirement.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Slack access, support expense, or limiting access based on demonstrated PyTorch competence.

r003.rationale: It recommends forums for conversational questions, but does not compare routine error-help requests with Slack.

r004.rationale: It does not mention Twitter or amplifying community projects.

sol-6.1.text:
I thought of user support as part of the product itself. You can have a great library, but if somebody gets stuck and can’t get help, that’s their experience of the library.

So we wanted different places for different kinds of conversations. GitHub issues were for bugs and concrete feature requests. The forums were a place where you could ask, “How do I do this?” and get an answer that other people could find later. And a chat channel could give you that more immediate interaction, where asking a small question feels easy.

The important thing was making those places welcoming and having the developers actually participate. Especially early on, answering a question wasn’t just helping one person—it was a way to understand what was confusing about the API or missing from the documentation. That feedback could then improve PyTorch itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes forums as searchable by other users, but does not identify search-engine indexability as a deliberate design requirement.

r002.rationale: It mentions chat as an immediate support channel, but says nothing about its expense or restricting Slack access based on demonstrated competence.

r003.rationale: It assigns how-to questions to forums and small questions to chat, but does not say routine error-help requests are better suited to forums than Slack.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention PyTorch’s Twitter account or amplifying community projects.
